newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian jail protest spread to seven cities.
newsitem.headline: Romanian jail protest spread to seven cities.

text.p: Protests by Romanian inmates denouncing overcrowded conditions spread on their fourth day to jails in seven cities, with convicts setting fire to the roof of one prison near the country's western border.
Inmates in Timisoara near the border with Serbia and Hungary set the roof of their prison ablaze but firefighters extinguished the fire without any injuries.
Protesters shouted slogans, banged metal cans against doors and refused food in Bucharest's main prison to denounce squalid conditions and tougher terms for parole.
They were joined by convicts in Turnu Severin on the Yugoslav border, Craiova in the southwest, Bacau and Iasi in the east and Tirgu Mures and Miercurea Ciuc in central Transylvania.

Prison officials reported no violence and protesters later settled down in their cells to watch a live broadcast on state television bringing face-to-face convicts' representatives and Justice Ministry officials.

"We started the protests over parole after the penal code extended the minimum term from six to eight months," a convict in his thirties told the television. "Pretty soon we'll be sleeping five or six to a bed instead of only three now."
Ministry officials said a wave of serious crimes in the post-communist era was to blame for overcrowding. Cash shortages were slowing construction of new prisons.
"We are not inviting people to jails," replied Ioan Chis, head of the Ministry's Jail Department. "You don't need to pass an entrance examination to be here."
Prisoners are demanding more family visits and complain about poor sanitation, with two latrines for several dozen people. They say conditions breed disease, violence and homosexual assaults.

Dorin Clocotici, Secretary of State at the Justice Ministry, told Reuters by telephone that the protests were coordinated with the intention of tarnishing Romania's image ahead of this week's visit by French President Jacques Chirac.
Official statistics put the number of inmates at 45,000, but Justice Ministry officials say the number of those in temporary or long-term custody reaches 100,000.
